items.cite: Camille Saint-Saëns, *Musical Memories*, trans. Edwin Gile Rich (Small, Maynard, 1919).
items.note: How did Saint-Saëns remember his childhood, the old Conservatoire, Liszt and the road to Samson et Dalila? His own account, with the story of the kettle’s oboe.

items.cite: Société Camille Saint-Saëns, *Chronologie*, 1835–1921 (website of the Société).
items.note: Where was he on a given day, and who wrote what to whom? A dated, letter-based chronology in eleven periods, with quotations from his letters and reviews.

items.cite: Sabina Teller Ratner, *Camille Saint-Saëns 1835–1921: A Thematic Catalogue of His Complete Works*, vol. 1: The Instrumental Works (Oxford University Press, 2002).
items.note: How were the concertos and symphonies written and published? The catalogue supplies the letters to Durand that Henle’s preface (linked) cites for the Fifth Piano Concerto.

items.cite: Hugh Macdonald, *Saint-Saëns and the Stage* (Cambridge University Press, 2019).
items.note: Why did Paris keep refusing his operas? Macdonald’s study of the operas, incidental music and film score; his Boston Symphony note (linked) is a short introduction to his view of the symphony.

items.cite: Arthur Dandelot, *La Vie et l’Œuvre de Saint-Saëns* (Paris, 1930).
items.note: What did his own circle say about the Egyptian Concerto? Dandelot records the composer’s remarks on its Andante and the first reviews, as cited in Henle’s preface (linked).
